This definition fits the physiological Unconscious, in which the brain is source and stage of the imaginings, but not the transcendental Unconscious, in which the brain is only the passively receiving stage of the imaginings. One can grant Hartmann only this: that precisely because of this identity of the stage, a mixture of the two series of phenomena often occurs, whereby the transcendental is physiologically contaminated. This is shown by the normal dream and by madness, but no longer by true somnambulism, in which the bodily sphere has been brought to silence. Precisely in the insane, however, there is shown — something our psychiatrists, to be sure, do not know, but which alone suffices to refute Hartmann — that their consciousness is intact as soon as they are placed into magnetic somnambulism. In the Unconscious, then, as Hartmann has defined it above, no soul can indeed be discovered. But no one has ever wanted to look for it there either. It can, however, be found in the more deeply lying Unconscious that Mesmer and his pupils discovered, and whose phenomena can be interpreted only in the sense of a metaphysical individualism. These facts have been known for a hundred years already — leaving antiquity quite aside — and therefore a "Philosophy of the Unconscious" that takes no account of them is an anachronism, because it does not maintain continuity in science. Hartmann's philosophy could indeed already have been refuted by Mesmer. The reader can now imagine what results when Hartmann applies the Unconscious, as he understands it, as a yardstick to the spiritistic phenomena. One half of them must then be explained crookedly, the other simply denied. And that is indeed what has happened. That Unconscious which shows itself prominently in magnetic somnambulism — namely the transcendental subject — would be far more equal to the task of explaining Spiritism from the medium than the physiologically Unconscious, which shows itself in dream, madness, and hysteria. And yet, although I thus have a more comprehensive explanatory principle ahead of Hartmann, I nevertheless hold it to be insufficient, and am, as the reader knows, compelled to shift a considerable part of the spiritistic phenomena onto an objective cause outside the medium, namely onto another order of beings. So too Aksakow. He too explains part of the phenomena from the medium, and calls these animistic. But the anima is for him far more than Hartmann's physiologically Unconscious; for him it is an individual soul with its own consciousness and with organizing powers. And yet he finds this anima insufficient to explain Spiritism. Aksakow, then, measures an object with a meter-stick and says the stick is too short; whereupon Hartmann takes a decimeter-stick and declares that this is long enough. It is as if one man said: 2×2 does not even make 5; the other, however: 2×2 makes even 6. Characteristic of Hartmann's manner of fencing is also his examination of the spiritistic problem of immortality, particularly with reference to pessimism. Now the view of the Spiritists is that the soul underlying the animistic phenomena outlasts death. The Spiritists further acknowledge earthly pessimism — that is, since this superlative is not applicable for want of an object of comparison — they acknowledge earthly evil. Earthly pessimism, however, flows for the Spiritists into a transcendental optimism, because, first, the doctrine of immortality satisfies the strongest instinct of man, the will to live; and because, second, the state beyond, although somnambulism gives us of it only a faint conception, appears as a relatively blessed one. That is why the magnetic somnambulists — whom Hartmann does not know — have always praised their state as a happy one and have not feared death, but rather the awakening, that is, the return to sensory consciousness. That is also why the Christian mystics have interpreted the ecstatic states as a "rapture into heaven." That is finally why the Indian mystic sees in ecstasy even a merging with Brahma, that is, a becoming God. For Hartmann, now, there exists no personal immortality. He does not concede that it exists; but he assumes it in order to be able to continue his academic investigation and to ask what would follow if our Unconscious were immortal. In doing so, however, he immediately again substitutes his own changeling for the transcendental subject, and now, of course, it is not difficult for him to let immortality flow into pessimism. He constructs a downright dreadful state beyond, roughly equivalent to a permanently declared hysteria and madness. Thus he seeks to create the appearance that the Spiritists themselves pour water onto his pessimistic mill. This procedure of Hartmann's — of foisting sheer nonsense onto his opponents' pen — runs through all his polemical writings. Here, however, the confusion of concepts lies quite openly exposed, by which he manages to throw the pessimistic cowl over Spiritism. But the Unconscious in Aksakow is something quite different from the Unconscious in Hartmann. In Aksakow the soul is something un-known by the sensory human being; in Hartmann — in that he concedes it only hypothetically — it is something unconscious in itself. Hartmann thus wishes to create the appearance of proceeding from the same premise as the Spiritists: the persistence of the Unconscious. But then he presents us as people who lack only logical sobriety in order to arrive at such a beyond — one which indeed follows from his Unconscious, but not from ours. The sober reader, however, will not let himself be dazzled by Hartmann's tract; as often as he comes upon the words "the Unconscious" and "the somnambulistic consciousness," he will tell himself that Hartmann means by them something other than the Spiritists do. I have said above, with regard to immortality, that man, already in this life, is unconsciously a spirit; but I have not said that he is an unconscious spirit. This, however, would have been my view in Hartmann's sense. He says: "If the spirit, as an individual, were to persist after death, it could only persist as absolutely unconscious; for if it loses the highest consciousness, that of the cerebral cortex, it will all the more certainly lose the lower consciousnesses, down to the cellular and atomic consciousness of its body.... But that which is allegedly supposed to be proved by them (the spiritistic experiences) — the persistence of memory-capable organic remnants without spirit and vital force — would furnish one of the most dreadful and repulsive chapters of pessimism, were one not entitled to dismiss it as a phantastical superstitious fabrication" (69, 72). We Spiritists, however, protest against the paternity of such a fabrication; the child is Hartmann's child, not ours. Likewise the alleged moral non-accountability of the spirits (74) holds only if the Unconscious meant by Hartmann were later to become a spirit; for, as is well known, the magnetic somnambulists — of whom Hartmann knows nothing — show not only an intellectual but also a moral enhancement. Finally Hartmann says: "From this point of view spiritistic practice appears as a bodily, spiritual, and moral danger, as a presumptuous game with dangerous and uncanny powers, without sense or purpose. Church and police would therefore have every reason to curb such reprehensible mischief with all their power, were they not right in preferring to leave this morbid excrescence of an overheated fantasy to the social power of natural healing and to medicine" (76). This ogling toward the police, however, amounts only to a confession of one's own inability to deal philosophically with Spiritism, and all that is now still lacking is the proposal of a press law forbidding philosophers in Germany to attack the dogmas issued by the philosophical papacy in Berlin. Under these circumstances it is surely not too harsh a judgment when I say that Hartmann's two anti-spiritistic tracts constitute a contribution to eristic, but none to philosophy. The spiritistic phenomena are, after all, facts. The opponents fight against these facts with mere arguments. But this is the act only of an inverted Don Quixote; for if it is superfluous to level a heavy lance against mere windmills, it is the height of folly to want to run one's head against a wall, and to declare realities impossible. However slowly people's habits of thought may change, it is nevertheless only a question of time before Spiritism finds its recognition. Its facts, however, now prove the existence of an individual soul and its persistence, and this view must necessarily influence, in the most favorable sense, our whole conception of the world and of life, and hence also our conduct of life. Aksakow, at the close of his preface, has posed a question to himself: "At the ebb of my life I sometimes ask myself: have I really done well to devote so much time, labor, and means to the study and dissemination of the phenomena of this field? Have I not taken a wrong path? Have I not chased after an illusion? Have I not lost an existence, without anything seeming to justify or repay my effort?" But to this question of Aksakow's no other answer can be given than the one he has given himself: "For the use of an earthly life there can be no more exalted purpose than to attempt to prove the transcendental nature of the human being, who is called to a far more exalted destiny than phenomenal existence!"
